new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Bongo has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Kilpatrick adds that the language is tonal (two phonemic tones) and that stress, if present, has no stated placement - compatible with the empty record, so 'refines'. Both quoted passages were verified against two independent scans (Rosetta djvu text layer and tesseract scanned of the OPSL 4 facsimile), which agree word for word. The live sil.org returned the an automated-access block on both attempts
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bongo is a two-tone language (phonemic H and L; phonetic mid is an allotone of L after H; falling tone only on long vowels or vowel clusters), with lexical tone contrasts on every syllable of mono-, di- and trisyllabic words. The paper has no stress section and gives no rule for where stress falls; its single mention says only that vowels of 'stressed syllables' are slightly lengthened and that the peak syllable of an utterance is lengthened as an intonational feature. Sec. 6.4 treats intonation at the sentence level (yes-no questions rising, statements and WH-questions falling). The TOC (pp. 1-2) lists no stress/accent heading, and pp. 50-62 (word list, notes, references) contain nothing on stress. The author flags 'prosodic features' as needing more investigation (p. 3).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only stress-related remark is the phonetic lengthening of stressed-syllable vowels (p. 33)
new_statements.identity_note: Kilpatrick 1985 describes the Tonj dialect (data gathered at Tonj from Gu Ba Kpuyu with Lynne Callinan, 1970s; note 6 records Bussere /r/ vs Tonj /l/ correspondences). Santandrea 1963, per Kilpatrick p. 3, bases its phonological summary on the Bussere dialect (the Wau-road community). Both are Bongo [bot] = bong1285.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress between the sources: only Kilpatrick 1985 could be opened, and it gives no placement rule. On tone there is a reported disagreement: Kilpatrick posits two phonemic tones (H, L; mid = allotone of L after H), while her note 12 (p. 61) says Santandrea 'posits three phonemic tones based on a single contrast', a contrast she could not replicate ('we could only elicit /hetira/ for body, and recorded different vowels for the other two words'). Santandrea's own text could not be opened (in copyright, HathiTrust search-only, no open copy anywhere found).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all fragments of the deciding quotation and the domain quote are verbatim in the scanned file we hold at the stated sections/lines; archive.org metadata confirms the item is Kilpatrick 1985, OPSL 4. (2) The deciding source is a dedicated descriptive phonology (62 pp) with a full tone chapter; it is the primary phonology in Glottolog's list (the 1979 entry is its unpublished draft). (3) I downloaded the three later SIL-South Sudan descriptions (Grammar Book 2018, 345 pp; Consonant and Vowel Book 2018, 72 pp; Dictionary 2018) from webonary: all analyse Bongo with five underlying lexical tone patterns on noun roots and tonal verb morphology, and none contains the word 'stress' or 'accent', which independently confirms the tonal coding with no stress rule.
